The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC:      
Objective for processing: 
This study is requesting HES data for the NIHR funded Doctoral Research Fellowship entitled: Quality of life is a matter of distance? - A study investigating the relationship between centralising health services and health inequalities for patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis & Osteoarthritis. 
In the UK the NHS has been moving in favour of centralising the care of its patients for certain specialised treatments.  Evidence has shown that this process can have a positive impact on the health outcomes of those patients treated in these specialised centers.  However, there are also drawbacks from increasing the distance that some patients have to travel to receive treatment.  A number of authors have documented the “distance decay” effect, whereby those that live further from the healthcare facilities that they need to access have lower rates of utilisation after adjustment for need than those who are closer, potentially negatively impacting on their health.  As the Acheson report (1998) argues “ all policies likely to have an impact on health should be evaluated in terms of their impact on health inequalities and formulated in such a way that by favoring the less well of they will, wherever possible reduce such inequalities”.  

The literature is growing for studies that have used a range of Geographical Information systems (GIS) techniques to map car and public transport travel times/ distances to healthcare facilities, however the link between this and the impact on an individual’s health is not routinely completed in many cases due to reasons such as a lack of linked health outcome data or a lack of knowledge about the healthcare facility attended.  This study provides an opportunity to fit into this gap using accurate HES hospital data (to accurately map patients journeys to healthcare) linked to health outcome data (PROMS) to investigate the relationship between distance and health outcomes and critically provide recommendations (on the potential impact of this on health outcomes) and guidance based on this for the future relocation of health services (whether shutting hospitals or creating specialised centres) to minimise the negative impacts.
  
The study is requesting HES data to answer the research question and test the studies hypothesis that:
Centralising hospital treatment will disproportionately affect those patients who live at a greater distance from the healthcare they need to attend and / or those that have limited transport accessibility resulting in an impact on health inequalities.

The study has applied for HES data as it provides both the home postcode of patients and the specific healthcare providers that they are accessing.   Access to this dataset will provide the most accurate information with which to undertake this study to produce results to inform policy.  It is focused specifically on adult (>17 years) osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis patients accessing outpatient and or inpatient appointments at Hospitals within West Yorkshire and Harrogate for the periods 2009/10, 2010/11 and 2011/12.  The study is requesting PROMS data and A & E data that have been collected for these identified patients over this period.  
The study has applied for home postcode data which is classed as patient identifiable to accurately calculate the distances and travel times of patients.  The starting point for a journey for a population with potential mobility issues will be critical, as it will influence whether the person can access the nearest bus stop and influence the route that a car journey could take.  This information would not be as accurate if the next level of data -  lower super output area (LSOA) is used in place of this (as this can contain on average 672 households across multiple roads).  There is a well-known phenomenon in geography called the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) whereby different results using the same data are achieved when data is aggregated thereby hiding some of the effects.  The study therefore has applied for the patients home postcode to provide the most accurate level of data.
Three years of data (2009/10, 2010/11 & 2011/12) has been requested for a number of reasons: Firstly, this will allow the study to focus on whether access to healthcare for patients changes over time (e.g. what is the average number of healthcare visits for an individual with rheumatoid arthritis), given that rheumatoid arthritis patients are likely to go through phases where no treatment is needed and then phases where intense treatment is required.  This means that taking 1 year may results in atypical findings.   Secondly, it will focus on whether patients are moving closer/ further away from the healthcare facilities that they are attending.  If the patient have just moved the impact on health of the distance/ travel time could be based on their previous location.  Thirdly, PROMS data is critical to allowing the relationship between quality of life and distance/ travel time to be investigated.  This is only available for hip, knee, varicose veins and hernia operations.  3 years of data of patients fitting the study criteria and having one of these operations has been estimated to provide a large enough population sample for the study to fully investigate the relationship.  

Processing activities: 
The data received will be stored securely.  The study is following the University of Leeds SEED Information Governance Policy
(http://medhealth.leeds.ac.uk/downloads/file/829/seed_information_governance_policy_v30).   
The HES data will be stored in the SEED system, a firewall protected area of the University of Leeds Storage Area Network. The study will be using STATA 13 and SPSS Software.
            
The study is processing the data in four stages:
Stage 1: Calculating the travel times and distances:
The first stage after receiving the data will be to accurately calculate the distances and travel times for the identified population of patients from their home postcode to each of the healthcare facilities that they have attended in the 3 years requested.  This will include the minimum variables required to calculate transport accessibility to the healthcare facilities (GP and Healthcare provider) and include the patient identifiable variable of home postcode.  The study has applied and got approval from the CAG for permission to have access to patient home postcode for this purpose.  The data required is:
Inpatient dataset: HES Patient identifier, HOMEADD, GPPRAC, PROCODE,PROCODET,ADMIDATE, DISDATE
Outpatient dataset: HES Patient Identifier, HOMEADD, GPPRAC, PROCODE,PROCODET, Appointment Date
A and E dataset: HES Patient Identifier, HOMEADD, GPPRAC, PROCODE,PROCODET, Arrivaldate, Arrivaltime.
In order to calculate the distances and travel times the study is using the software Visography TRACC (http://www.basemap.co.uk/tracc/) and software ArcGIS).  This software uses the ITN road network, traffic master speed data, Urban pathways network, public transport stop data, public transport scheduling data alongside the patients postcode data from  the HES dataset, date of the appointment  and postcode of healthcare facility attended to calculate the shortest distance and fastest travel times.  The distances and travel times will be calculated for each patient trip identified in the HES dataset that has been received.  This will mean that there will be multiple trips per patient across the 3 years and potentially to a range of hospitals (which will all need to be calculated).  The resulting data produced will be accessed and analysed through and saved on the University SEED system.  
After this point the patient identifiable variable home postcode will be destroyed and will not be required.
Stage 2: What are the healthcare and transport accessibility needs of patients with Osteoarthritis and Rheumatoid Arthritis?
This stage will use the distances and travel times calculated in stage 1 and develop a descriptive narrative about the patients, focusing on how far patients are travelling, when and how frequently they are travelling and whether this depends on comorbidities / changes by gender/ age etc.. (using the full dataset requested, excluding the patients home postcode).  The data will be analysed using the STATA software.  Analysis will include; average number of hospital visits for patients with Osteoarthritis or Rheumatoid Arthritis and whether these changes by gender, age, ethnicity etc…, and Average distance travelled to hospital and annual distance as recorded by the total distance per patient over a year period.  It will also include a documentation of the types of treatment that patients are accessing hospital for over the 3 year period.      
The data from the HES will be utilised alongside information that will be collected in parallel about the disease pathways from clinicians based at Chapel Allerton Hospital (e.g information on treatments and severity that could be expected for patients with Osteoarthritis or Rheumatoid Arthritis), transport officials and the studies public patient involvement group that has been set up to look at the needs of patients. 
For clarity, no patient specific data is being accessed from Chapel Allerton Hospital.  The links are with the clinicians to document the typical treatment pathway – e.g. what should a typical patient with Rheumatoid Arthritis expect in terms of treatment when they are going through an episode.  This will help with determining the expected treatment codes from the HES dataset.   The output will be a detailed narrative of the population that has been requested in terms of their healthcare needs, but also critically their transport accessibility levels.  
Stage 3: The relationship between distance/ travel time and health outcomes (using the sample of patients where PROMS data has been collected and the Charlson comorbidity Index, which is determined for all) and the ELSA dataset.
Stage 3 will model the relationship between distance/ travel times (as calculated in stage 1) and quality of life (as measured using the PROMS data and the Charlson comorbidity index).    The data will be analysed using univariate and multivariate regression models using the statistical software STATA 13.  In these models quality of life will be the dependent variable and travel times/ distance the key independent variables.  Research has shown that key variables that should be included alongside distance/ travel time in the model (that have also been requested from the HES dataset) are: deprivation (as measured using the index of multiple deprivations), gender, age, ethnicity, rural/urban indicator, comorbidities and month of year.  Including these additional variables will allow the study to control for potential confounding effects when focusing on the relationship between distance/ travel time and quality of life / health.  The outputs will show statistically whether there is a distance decay effect – does the quality of life of a patient get worse the further they live from the healthcare facilities that they need to attend and by how much.  The models and results from them will be used as the basis for the publications planned and wider dissemination activities in addition to contributing to the PhD thesis.
In addition to the statistical modelling that will be undertaken using the HES PROMS dataset the study has also planned to utilise the English Longitudinal Study on Ageing (ELSA) to do additional statistical modelling to inform the study.  This dataset will be accessed through NATCEN.  This dataset has a wider range of quality of life variables (e.g. BMI, CASP19 etc…) and socio demographic variables (e.g. incomes, whether an individual is living alone, access to car etc…), but is based on a representative sample of 12,000 >50 year olds across the whole of England and does not have information on the healthcare facilities attended (unlike the HES dataset).  2,600 individuals in the survey have Osteoarthritis and 700 Rheumatoid Arthritis.  The dataset is not currently linked to HES data.  The study will use this dataset of patients to model the impact of distance/ travel time to the nearest healthcare facility on the additional quality of life variables (therefore allowing a comparison using different variables and to the HES PROMS dataset).  
 At no point in the future will data be linked to the patient level data that has been requested.  When the study applies for the ELSA data from NATCEN no links will be made to the HES-PROMS data that is being applied for in this application. The two datasets are being requested for separate aspects of the study.      
Stage 4: Applying the evidence to scenarios and key questions
The results of the models in stage 3 will be applied to the stage 2 population for a number of scenarios.  This stage will focus on the implication of changing the location of some of the current services and look at optimal service location.  Using the distance and travel time data for the patients in stage 2 (accessed through the SEED facility) what would be the predicted impact of changing where they attended the healthcare facilities on their quality of life?   For example, for all the patients attending the LGI hospital in Leeds for treatment - what impact would adding the additional travel distance to get to Bradford hospital have on their quality of life?   Alternatively, if 24 hour GP surgeries are implemented which would be the closest GP surgery for the patients to attend (using the HES data) at the weekend and what would be the impact if they had to attend an alternative in the area using the results of the modelling – what would be the optimal location?  
 These scenarios are being developed in conjunction with the studies advisory board and public patient involvement group.
These will include, for example:
•           What would be the impact on health outcomes from changing those patients who access their rheumatoid arthritis treatment from Chapel Allerton Hospital (as a group) in Leeds to Harrogate hospital or more widely Newcastle or Birmingham?  Thus measuring the impact of changing the distance/ travel time (evidence from stage 3) on health.
•           Where would be the optimal location (in terms of reducing health inequalities) for a new healthcare facility for the current set of patients?
•           Are different disease group affected differently – Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis
•           What is an acceptable (threshold) travel time/ distance to healthcare for patients with osteoarthritis/ rheumatoid arthritis?
The results of this stage will feed into key planned dissemination activities, be posted on the study website and contribute to the PhD thesis chapters.
No data will be linked to the patient level data that has been requested. 
Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
A number of outputs are planned from this data.  At all stages it is planned that the studies outputs prior to publication will be discussed with the studies public patient involvement group – which consist of 5 people who have either osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis and 1 has both.  
1.  The data is being requested for an NIHR Doctoral Research Fellowship.  The thesis will be submitted by the end of March 2018.
2.    As documented in the study protocol a number of journal papers and conference presentations are planned over the 4 years of the study:
External conference presentations including:
•           The study will be presented as a poster at the NIHR trainee meeting (November 2015).  The theme of this meeting is making a difference – from evidence to impact.
•           The modelling element of the study will be presented as a presentation at the Health and Economics Study Group (July 2016 target date).  This will document the initial results of modelling the relationship between quality of life and distance/ travel times to healthcare.
•           What is the effect on health of changing where patients access healthcare (target date 2017)  Festival of Public health: Manchester
Journal Papers including:
•           When, how far and how often do patients with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis access healthcare.  A population study.  – To be submitted to the Journal of Health and Place. (Planned June 2016 target date).  This will provide the results of stage 2 of the processing  - the narrative
•           Calculating access to healthcare – does it matter what method you use?  - To be submitted to the journal of Transport and Health (Target date – summer 2016)
•           Distance travelled for treatment of Osteoarthritis/ Rheumatoid Arthritis: who travels the furthest and does it impact on the outcome?   - to be submitted to the journal of Health Economics (Target July 2017)
•           How does distance impact on health: the centralization argument?  - to be submitted to BMJ (Target Jan 2018)
The study has included funds in the budget to cover open access publication.  This will mean that the journal papers will be free and open to members of the public.  In addition the study will be presented at internal seminars and conferences at the University of Leeds.  

3.  The study will be disseminated into the National and local policy arena, which will be aided by the members of the advisory board for this study and the public patient involvement group.  
•           The study advisory board includes leading clinicians in the area of musculoskeletal conditions including- the Director of the Leeds Musculoskeletal Biomedical Research Unit at Chapel Allerton Hospital.  The study has links with the public patient involvement group based in this unit.
•           The study advisory board includes the Lead for Public Health in the Leeds PCT and the Director of Public Health at Leeds City Council.  Who’s providing input into the study and will help to promote the study outside of the University.
•           The Department for Transport have requested a presentation of the study findings at a later date.  This department currently provides guidance on accessibility planning.  
•           5 members of the public who have either osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis or both are included in a public patient involvement group.  One of the key tasks of working with this group is to aid in the appropriate dissemination of the research beyond academic publications. 

4.  The following website has been developed to both promote the study before getting the data (ex ante) and will promote the work that is completed in a public facing format.
http://www.distancetohealthcare.leeds.ac.uk/

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
There is currently little evidence on the impact of centralising health services on health inequalities from the perspective of the changes in the distance/ transport accessibility that some patients would have to endure to access healthcare services.  This is an issue, as locations of current and future healthcare services are being planned along with the transport networks and bus routes, but not always together.
The benefit from the knowledge gained through this study is that this can form part of the decision making process when services are relocated or new facilities opened and a method to minimize the impact on health inequalities, where inequalities have been identified (e.g. targeted community transport services).  There is support for this level of analysis – local authorities (prior to the public health remit - following the abolishment of the PCTs) have been required to undertake accessibility planning to healthcare services, but this has taken the simplistic form of what percentage of the population can access the hospital in 1 hours travel time and is not based on actual healthcare facilities attended or the potential health outcomes from this.  The method applied in this study making full use of the HES data will change the accuracy of the results and provide decision makers with a tangible health outcome based on locations that can used to make decisions about treatment locations and where services should be located to minimize inequalities in health across the country.  
This has major implications not only in terms of the locations of healthcare services, but also the potential benefits to patients.  Research identified in the systematic review undertaken by this study have identified that there is evidence of a distance decay effect – patients are less likely to attend follow up appointments, attend screening appointments, have later diagnosis of disease, stay in hospital for longer periods of times and have fewer visitors and as a result a worse prognosis the further they live from the healthcare services that they need to attend.   Identifying these patients and reducing this impact will be a benefit.  
The models developed in this study will allow the implications of different restructuring configurations of the NHS services for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid Arthritis patients on health inequalities to be examined. It would then be straightforward to extend the scope of this model to focus on other diseases (e.g. cardiovascular, diabetes).  
This study was funded through the rigorous selection process of the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) doctoral fellowship scheme, against the key criteria that this study will have impact in the NHS.  The study was developed in conjunction with leading clinicians in the area of arthritis and members of the studies public patient involvement group to ensure that the study met this criteria.   
Key outputs will provide the NHS with robust recommendations on the impact of the distance/ time taken for patients travel to healthcare facilities and the impact on their health and well - being. Recommendations for reducing health inequalities that result from issues related to accessibility to healthcare services will be disseminated to key stakeholders with the aim of informing policy (as discussed above).   If these recommendations are acted upon the benefits to patients will be more equitable access to healthcare services and a method for analysing the impacts of transport accessibility on the decision.
The study will be completed in March 2018.  Results will be disseminated directly, into the Department for Transport and Department of Health at a national level, local authorities at a local level and the hospitals that the study is working with in order to inform policy and decisions made, at the points at which they are completed.
